title: Are MCPs Overhyped? A Rant about MCPs — Henry Mao, Smithery

summary: Henry Mao, founder and CEO of Smithery and a member of the MCP steering committee, presents a high-level critique of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) ecosystem rather than a technical deep dive. He begins with his origin story: in November 2024, he explored the ARC AGI challenge—an IQ test for LLMs where humans achieve roughly 80% accuracy but LLMs historically struggled. OpenAI's o3 release achieved human-level performance on this benchmark, raising expectations that autonomous agents would solve real-world tasks. However, by 2025, Henry observes what he calls Claude's paradox—frontier labs produce impressive intelligence that remains trapped in a box, requiring context and capability (inputs and outputs) to become practically useful. Anthropic released MCP in November 2024 as an open standard to connect LLMs to services, but the emerging ecosystem surfaced new problems. Henry categorizes MCP user problems as fragmentation (growing number of servers, difficulty finding quality ones; the MCP committee is working on an official registry but reputation remains an open question), high installation friction with multi-step processes, security concerns, and the lack of a plan for agentic payments. Developer problems include hosting challenges (despite Streamable HTTP transport easing some issues), limited tooling (only a basic MCP inspector exists), distribution and discoverability, observability, and monetization. Smithery, founded December 2024, aims to be an AI gateway to orchestrate AI-native services. Henry demos the Smithery playground, showing an agent searching servers, connecting to GitHub and Linear MCPs, finding the most pressing GitHub issue, and creating a Linear ticket. He concludes with a vision of the internet dominated by tool calls rather than clicks, where agent experience matters more than user experience.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction & Background
sections.summary: Henry Mao introduces himself as founder/CEO of Smithery, MCP steering committee member, and co-founder of Jenny AI. He previews a high-level rant about MCP ecosystem problems rather than a technical deep dive.

sections.title: Origin Story & Claude's Paradox
sections.summary: Henry recounts tackling the ARC AGI challenge in November 2024, which OpenAI's o3 soon dominated. Despite model intelligence advances, autonomous agents remain absent from practical use—Claude's paradox where intelligence is stuck in a box. Anthropic released MCP to address this.

sections.title: User Problems with MCP
sections.summary: Fragmentation makes finding quality MCP servers difficult; an official registry is in progress but reputation remains unsolved. Other issues include high install friction, security concerns, and lack of agentic payment infrastructure.

sections.title: Developer Problems with MCP
sections.summary: Developers face hosting challenges, limited tooling (only basic MCP inspector), distribution and discoverability gaps, observability concerns, and monetization questions.

sections.title: Smithery Solution & Demo
sections.summary: Smithery, founded December 2024, aims to be an AI gateway for AI-native services. Demo shows an agent connecting GitHub and Linear MCPs to find pressing issues and create tickets automatically.

sections.title: Vision & Conclusion
sections.summary: Henry envisions a future internet dominated by tool calls rather than clicks, where agent experience matters more than user experience, built collaboratively by the developer community.

demonstrations: Smithery playground: an agent finds the most pressing issue on a GitHub repository and creates a Linear ticket by connecting to two different MCPs
limitations: Registry alone will not solve fragmentation—reputation scoring for quality MCPs remains an open question
No plan exists for agentic payments or AI-native service economy
Developer tooling is basic with only the MCP inspector available
Demo only scratches the surface of what is possible
